market.title: How DER SPIEGEL addresses subscriber churn, part 1: building a score
market.summary_raw: Like most news publishers worldwide, Germany’s DER SPIEGEL sees reducing subscriber churn as a major priority. For many publishers, finding ways to retain their current subscribers is even more important than acquiring new ones.
market.content_text: In this three-part series, Alexander Held, Lead Data Science at DER SPIEGEL in Hamburg, describes how his team built a model that estimates each subscriber’s risk of cancelling, put it to the test in a retention experiment, and asked subscribers why they stay or leave. Part one covers the model and how well it works. By Alexander Held A machine learning model scores each active digital subscription with the probability that the subscriber will churn in the next two months. The question is not whether someone cancels this particular subscription, but whether they are gone entirely, without returning on a different one. The model is not built to catch every future churner. It is built to produce a group whose average churn probability sits far above the base rate, so retention work can be aimed at a defined set of people instead of the whole base. The data and the model We score full-price digital subscriptions. As training data we use three kinds of signal, cross-device on all logged-in sessions: Subscription data: Tenure of the current subscription, subscription type, payment method, price increases experienced, number of previous trials and subscriptions, earlier cancellations. Engagement data: Our internal engagement score at four horizons, now and one, three and six months back, plus a trend signal. Behavioural data: Articles read to the end, scroll depth, page views per visit, active days. The strongest predictors are tenure of the current subscription (19.3% of feature importance), article scroll depth (7.6%), total time paid across all subscriptions past and present (6.7%) and scrolls per visit (4.8%). The top 10 features together account for roughly 55% of the total. Surprisingly, no version of our own engagement score makes the top five. How long someone has paid, and whether they finish what they open, predicts churn better than our engagement metric. Our survey pointed the same way, and part three of this article series has more on it. On these features we train a gradient boosting model, and then calibrate it, so the output reads as a real probability rather than a ranking. We also split the data by time, not at random. The model learns on one date, is calibrated on a later one and tested months after that, so it has to predict forward the way it does in production. Evaluation Our headline figure is an AUC of 0.82, measured on a held out test set. For those who don’t know, AUC is defined as a bet: pick one subscriber who left and one who stayed at random, and in 82% of those pairs the model gave the higher score to the one who left. Guessing would land at 50%, a flawless model at 100%. The model then hands us a probability per subscription, ranking the base of full price digital subscriptions from safest to most at risk. We then drew the line at a 15% churn probability. That came close to 10,000 subscriptions and they churn at 28% against a base rate of around 4%, seven times as high. It holds about 36% of everyone who leaves. […]

market.title: How we got 40,000 young women to read about the Strait of Hormuz
market.summary_raw: A Swedish newsletter brand is quietly proving something the industry keeps saying it believes: the relationship is the product. Here's what we're learning and why we're now building a second brand on the same foundation.
market.content_text: By Irena Pozar and Martin Schori For the past decade, most of us in news media have been trying to answer the same question: what do we put behind the paywall? Another question could be: how do we get people to really want to engage with our products – a nd want it enough to pay, return, reply, and stay? We are writing this from inside a small Swedish media company called Hint , which just turned one year old. Here, one of our products is starting to answer that question in a way we think is worth sharing. The numbers Hint is a daily newsletter. It goes to 40,000 subscribers, 85% of them are women, 50% are between 25-45 years old. The open rate is 70%. Those subscribers read about the Strait of Hormuz, major arms deals, domestic politics, and the rest of the news agenda, alongside lighter material. It’s an engaged group, they reply to emails and answer our polls. Every day. (Not all of them, obviously.) Ad sales are now running, and we just did our first hire. We have, so far, done something that the entire Western news industry says it wants to do: bring young women back to news. We did it, we believe, by building a direct relationship with a clearly defined audience – and talking to them like a real person . Why most news media struggle to do this Many people believe that news is neutral in the sense that it lacks gender codes. We would argue that most major news sites are male-coded. We know, we have worked there for decades. And during these decades we’ve optimised our sites, our front pages, our notification logic, our subject mix and our tone of voice for the audience we already have – which, across most legacy newsrooms in the West, skews older and male – and then we’ve been surprised that the audiences we don’t have don’t show up. We do not believe that we need to cover other stuff in order to reach these audiences. In Hint, the journalism about Hormuz is the same journalism as elsewhere. What changes is who it’s written to, in what voice, in what container, and inside what relationship. Martin Schori speaking at WAN-IFRA’s Newsroom Summit last week at VG headquarters in Oslo. Photo by Tom Atle Bordevik / Bordevik.no What this looks like in practice Hint works because the relationship was built first and the business model second. The daily inbox is the product. The reply button is part of the product. The voice — informal, specific, recognisably one person writing to another — is also the product. The 70% open rate is a signal that the relationship is real. We’re now building a second brand on top of what Hint taught us. It’s called 08 — the dialing area code for Stockholm — a membership-funded newsletter about the city. We’re taking what works at Hint (voice, direct relationship through email, community thinking) and combining it with original local journalism, somewhere in the territory of The Mill in Manchester. Two months after launch we’re at 2.500 signups. 08 is explicitly membership-based, not subscription-based. […]
